course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Transoceanic Interconnections
unit.description: Study how new maritime technology, state-sponsored voyages, the Columbian Exchange, and coerced labor connected the world's oceans and reshaped societies.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.5 key concept: the demand for labor intensified, and colonial economies in the Americas depended on coerced labor such as the encomienda, hacienda, and Spanish adaptation of the mit'a
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing labor systems in Spanish America, c. 1500–1700
stimulusBlocks.text:
Under the encomienda system, the Spanish crown granted colonists the right to demand labor and tribute from Indigenous communities, in return for protecting them and teaching them Christianity. Abuses were widespread, and the crown restricted the system after the 1540s. Large estates called haciendas later relied on Indigenous workers bound by debt.

In the Andes, Spanish officials adapted the Inca mit'a. Communities had to send a share of their adult men to work for months in the silver mines of Potosí, discovered in 1545. The work was dangerous, and many workers died from accidents and mercury poisoning.

questions.prompt: The adaptation of the mit'a best illustrates
choices: the end of all coerced labor in the Andes
change in the form of the labor draft combined with continuity in its purpose
continuity in form combined with change in purpose and conditions
complete continuity with Inca practice
questions.explanation: The rotating draft continued, but it now served deadly colonial mining.
choiceExplanations: Coerced labor continued.
The rotating form continued while the purpose changed.
The rotating draft continued, but it now served deadly colonial mining.
Conditions and purpose changed greatly.
questions.distinguisher: The order is reversed: the form stayed similar, while the purpose changed to colonial mining.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.5 key concept: the Atlantic trading system involved the movement of goods, wealth, and free and unfree laborers, and chattel slavery grew with plantation economies
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the growth of the Atlantic slave trade, c. 1500–1750
stimulusBlocks.text:
Sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean demanded huge amounts of labor. As Indigenous populations collapsed, planters turned to enslaved Africans. Over the course of the transatlantic slave trade, about 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships, and nearly 2 million died during the Middle Passage. Most went to Brazil and the Caribbean.

Atlantic slavery differed from many earlier forms of slavery. Enslaved status was inherited and tied to race, and enslaved people were treated as property, a system called chattel slavery. Yet enslaved Africans kept languages, beliefs, and skills, including rice cultivation, that shaped American societies.

questions.explanation: The passage says status was inherited, tied to race, and treated people as property.
choiceExplanations: Slavery existing earlier is not a difference.
Chattel slavery treated people as property.
The passage says status was inherited, tied to race, and treated people as property.
All slavery involved forced labor.
questions.distinguisher: Forced labor was common to all slavery, so it cannot be the difference.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did historians call the Manila trade the first truly global network?
choices: It was the first trade between China and Southeast Asia
It ended trade across the Indian Ocean
It linked Africa and Europe by sea for the very first time in history
It linked the Americas, Asia, and Europe through one trade

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.5 key concept: the global flow of silver from the Americas and Japan, much of it to China, connected maritime empires and Asian economies
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing the global silver trade, c. 1550–1700
stimulusBlocks.text:
After 1571, when Spain founded Manila in the Philippines, ships called the Manila galleons carried silver from Mexico across the Pacific. In Manila, Chinese merchants traded silk and porcelain for the silver. China's economy had a huge demand for silver, partly because the Ming government collected taxes in it.

Historians describe this as the first truly global trade network, linking the Americas, Asia, and Europe. The flood of silver also caused inflation in Spain, which spent much of its wealth on wars and imports instead of investing at home.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, one effect of the silver trade on Spain was
choices: falling prices as silver left Spain
inflation as silver flowed in
rapid industrial growth
the end of Spanish wars in Europe
questions.explanation: The flood of silver raised prices in Spain.
choiceExplanations: Silver caused inflation.
The flood of silver raised prices in Spain.
Spain spent silver on wars and imports, not industry.
Spain kept fighting wars.
questions.distinguisher: Prices rose, not fell, as American silver entered Spain.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.5 key concept: some Asian states, such as Tokugawa Japan and Qing China, sought to limit the disruptive effects of European trade through restrictive policies
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing Japanese and Chinese limits on European trade, c. 1630–1760
stimulusBlocks.text:
In the 1630s, the Tokugawa shogunate banned Christianity, expelled Portuguese traders, and forbade Japanese from traveling abroad. Only Dutch and Chinese merchants were allowed to trade, and the Dutch were confined to a small island in Nagasaki harbor. Japan continued to trade with China and Korea.

The Qing also controlled European trade. By the 1750s, European merchants were limited to the port of Canton and could deal only with licensed Chinese merchant houses. Both states welcomed some trade but tried to keep foreign influence under control.

allowed unlimited trade with Europeans

questions.explanation: Both permitted trade in limited places and under strict rules.
choiceExplanations: Each allowed some European trade.
Both kept control of their ports.
Both strictly limited trade.
Both permitted trade in limited places and under strict rules.
questions.distinguisher: Both allowed some European trade: the Dutch at Nagasaki and merchants at Canton.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 4.5 key concept: silver from the Americas and coerced labor linked the economies of the Americas, Europe, and China
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing silver mining and trade, c. 1545–1650
stimulusBlocks.text:
In 1545 Spanish miners found a mountain of silver at Potosí, in the Andes of present-day Bolivia. To obtain labor, the Spanish adapted the Inca mit'a into a system in which Indigenous communities had to send a share of their men to work in the mines for pay far below the value of the silver they produced. Mining relied on mercury, and many miners died from accidents and poisoning.

Much of the silver crossed the Atlantic to Spain, but a large share went to China by way of the Manila galleons, because Chinese merchants demanded silver for silk and porcelain. Historians note that the silver trade tied together the economies of the Americas, Europe, and China.

Spain kept all of the silver from its colonies in its own treasury
Mining at Potosí had little effect on the Indigenous communities

questions.explanation: Silver flowed from the Americas to Spain and, through Manila, to China.
choiceExplanations: The passage describes silver moving to China, not from it.
The passage says a large share of the silver went to China.
The passage says many miners died and communities had to send men to the mines.
Silver flowed from the Americas to Spain and, through Manila, to China.
questions.distinguisher: Spain received much silver, but the passage shows that a large share did not stay there.
